extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research integrity officers, and institutional officials dealing with authorship and misconduct adjudication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative criteria for assigning authorship, resolving authorship disputes, and adjudicating research misconduct—especially in cases of retraction and resubmission. Covers ethical norms (fairness, accountability, honesty, transparency, integrity), procedural recommendations, and aggravating/mitigating factors for sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit should be given where credit is due and only where it is due; authorship credit should be awarded for significant contributions; those who are not named as authors but who have contributed to the research should be acknowledged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorary authorship and ghost authorship are unethical because they either give credit where it is not due or fail to give credit where it is due; ghost authorship can be equated with plagiarism. Fairness may be interpreted differently in disputes and is contextual and discipline-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of named contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors to the research should be named as authors or mentioned in acknowledgments so others know who did the work if questions arise about quality, reproducibility, or integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should take responsibility for their research and be able to explain what they did and why. Naming contributors supports accountability by enabling explanation and follow-up when issues arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in authorship lists and contribution statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship lists and contribution statements (including 'contributed equally' designations) must reflect the truth about what happened in a research project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honorary authorship exaggerates or fabricates contributions; ghost authorship conceals them. Contribution statements should not misrepresent roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of contributions and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific and technical contributions, and financial and other forms of support, should be fully disclosed and described in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure promotes accountability and helps mitigate bias and competing interests. Omitting contributors to hide financial interests can impair trustworthiness. Transparency includes clear explanation of contributions if authorship changes after retraction/resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance threshold for authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship should be granted for 'significant' contributions, though what counts as 'significant' is not precisely defined and is often contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may list roles (e.g., data collection, research design) that qualify, but detailed specifications are discipline- and context-dependent. Determinations of significance require case-by-case judgment and may rely on norms or contributor taxonomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contributor taxonomies (CRediT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) distinguishes multiple categories of activities contributors may perform and can be required by journals to describe contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRediT (14 roles) clarifies who did what and can supplement authorship decisions but does not, by itself, define or replace authorship. It can be used to explain contributions and the reasons for authorship/acknowledgement decisions, including when a paper is revised after retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments for including a contributor who committed misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person made a significant contribution but committed misconduct, arguments for including them as an author include fairness (credit where due), accountability, honesty, and transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listing the contributor can help explain work if questions arise and preserve the historical record. Use of CRediT and explanatory notes (about the retraction and revisions) can help satisfy other norms while acknowledging misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments against including a contributor who committed misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterarguments include that denying authorship can be fair if the person does not deserve to benefit from misconduct; including them may morally taint the research and harm coauthors' reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other norms (accountability, honesty, transparency) might be met by detailed acknowledgments and CRediT statements rather than authorship. Aggravating/mitigating factors (intent, career stage, harm) influence judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudication of misconduct must treat similar cases similarly and impose sanctions proportional to the seriousness of the transgressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness (formal principle of justice) supports consistency and is linked to institutional integrity. Sanction proportionality should consider aggravating and mitigating factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors for sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider include the person's intent (intentional/knowing/reckless), career stage (trainee/junior/senior), prior history of misconduct, evidence of a pattern, impact of the misconduct (harm), and the institution's responsibility (training/guidance provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors help determine sanction severity; e.g., intentional falsification by a senior investigator harming participants warrants more severe sanctions than reckless falsification by a trainee causing no harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterrence as a sanctioning norm
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions should be likely to deter others from similar misconduct; publicizing findings and sanctions enhances deterrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deterrence can conflict with fairness (e.g., imposing harsh penalties to send a message). Agencies like ORI publish case summaries to promote deterrence and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in misconduct policies and findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and funding agencies should make misconduct policies, procedures, and findings available to researchers and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish policies and, when appropriate, case summaries. However, avoid publicizing proceedings until they are complete to prevent unnecessary reputational harm and confidentiality violations. NSF and ORI have different publication practices (e.g., ORI names individuals; NSF closeout memoranda do not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability of institutions and corrective actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should hold individuals and institutions accountable and take actions to redress harms (e.g., correct the research record, revise policies, increase training, support whistleblowers, audit records, compensate harmed subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correcting the research record (retraction, correction, republication) is a key redress. Accountability recognizes that collaborators, supervisors, and institutions may share responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional integrity and consistent administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must develop and follow policies and procedures for research ethics and administer them consistently, impartially, and transparently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining institutional integrity is crucial because violations can undermine other research norms. Weaponization of misconduct allegations (e.g., using them to settle authorship disputes) risks harming institutional integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate locus for resolving authorship disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship disputes are best resolved by the corresponding author with concurrence of the research group; administrative (institutional) removal of authorship should be a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may provide mediation resources (ombudspersons, ethics staff) but adjudication (sanctions) is the responsibility of independent parties (institution/funders). Administrative denial of authorship risks weaponization and should be used cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting the scientific record (retraction/correction/republication)
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct undermines results, correcting the record can involve retracting or correcting publications; retraction-and-republication is a mechanism to correct pervasive errors while preserving reliable underlying work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should consider explanatory notes about authorship changes on resubmission; retraction policies (and expressions of concern) play roles in transparency and redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Move toward contributor model
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a contributor model where major contributors are authors and all other contributors are named with careful descriptions of their contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contributor model could reduce the premium on authorship and help resolve ethical dilemmas by providing meaningful recognition for non-author contributors; may be aided by CRediT and supplementary acknowledgments if journals have space constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal policies to promote responsible authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should require contribution descriptions, signed statements affirming authorship criteria have been met, and may require use of contributor taxonomies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such policies help promote responsible authorship but do not fully resolve disputes about significance; journals could also require explanatory notes when authorship changes after retraction/resubmission.
